articles.title: WeatherTech founder might be the newest US consumer protection official
articles.summary: The car mat CEO has committed to US-based manufacturing.
articles.body: President Donald Trump made an unconventional pick for his nomination to the Federal Trade Commission: WeatherTech founder and CEO David MacNeil. MacNeil founded the company, which makes weather-resistant car floor mats, in 1989, according to its website, and he owns 100 percent of the company. WeatherTech has made it a mission to keep its manufacturing and workforce in the US. FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson congratulated MacNeil on X and called him an “outstanding businessman and great patriot,” sharing a clip from a news segment where MacNeil shared his commitment to manufacturing in the US. If confirmed, MacNeil become the third member of the panel, taking the seat formerly held by Melissa Holyoak, who is now a US Attorney in Utah. MacNeil’s background is somewhat unusual for an FTC commissioner. Many come from legal and academic backgrounds, or have experience working on Capitol Hill. MacNeil is a reported billionaire who recently bought a $75 million mansion in a town near Trump’s Mar-a-Lago. He’s a Republican donor who has supported Trump, though notably in 2018 threatened to withhold donations from candidates who refused to support the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program. Still, his experience may fit with some of the FTC’s current enforcement and regulatory goals, such as enforcing the Made in the USA Labeling Rule, to prevent deceptive marketing. MacNeil will need to be confirmed by the Senate, where Democrats will likely take issue with Trump’s failure to nominate Democrats to the typically five member panel after firing two of them against Supreme Court precedent.

articles.title: Carreta com 45 toneladas de sal bloqueia trânsito em Feira de Santana | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente aconteceu na manhã desta terça-feira (10), na região da Avenida Papa João XXIII, afetando o trânsito nas proximidades da rotatória de acesso ao bairro Tomba.
articles.summary: Acidente aconteceu na manhã desta terça-feira (10), na região da Avenida Papa João XXIII, afetando o trânsito nas proximidades da rotatória de acesso ao bairro Tomba.
articles.body:
Uma carreta bitrem carregada com aproximadamente 45 toneladas de sal ficou atravessada na pista na manhã desta terça-feira (10), no final da Avenida João Durval, em Feira de Santana , segunda maior cidade da Bahia. A situação provocou congestionamento na região e afetou o trânsito na Avenida Papa João XXIII, nas proximidades da rotatória de acesso ao bairro Tomba.

De acordo com informações apuradas pela TV Subaé, no local, o motorista, que não é de Feira de Santana, teria pedido orientação a um motociclista para chegar ao destino. Ao seguir a rota indicada, a carreta acabou ficando travada na pista, sem conseguir avançar.

Equipes da Superintendência Municipal de Trânsito (SMT) foram acionadas e estiveram no local para organizar o fluxo de veículos e orientar os condutores. O trânsito foi liberado após a retirada da carreta, que ocorreu por volta das 16h.

Como lembra o superintendente da SMT, Ricardo Cunha, a circulação de veículos de grande porte, como bitrens, em áreas urbanas com intenso fluxo de veículos e pedestres, representa riscos de acidentes e pode provocar a obstrução de vias importantes.

Carreta bitrem tomba na Papa João XXIII, em Feira de Santana. — Foto: Fotos: Divulgação/SMT

O caso também reforça a fiscalização sobre a circulação de veículos pesados no perímetro urbano. Segundo a SMT, motoristas e transportadoras que desrespeitarem as restrições estão sujeitos às penalidades previstas no Código de Trânsito Brasileiro (CTB) e na legislação municipal.

articles.title: Reportagem do g1 vence Prêmio Abapa de Jornalismo 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: Jornalista João Souza conquistou o troféu na modalidade 'Internet' com a reportagem 'O novo algodão baiano: a tecnologia que está mudando a produção da semente ao mercado'.
articles.summary: Jornalista João Souza conquistou o troféu na modalidade 'Internet' com a reportagem 'O novo algodão baiano: a tecnologia que está mudando a produção da semente ao mercado'
articles.body:
Jornalista João Souza vence Prêmio Abapa de Jornalismo 2026, na modalidade internet — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

O jornalista João Souza , do g1 , venceu o Prêmio Abapa de Jornalismo 2026 , nesta terça-feira (10), em Salvador , com a reportagem " O novo algodão baiano: a tecnologia que está mudando a produção da semente ao mercado ".

O texto explica como o algodão baiano vive uma transformação que combina genética, tecnologia, dados e rastreabilidade para aumentar a produtividade e a qualidade da produção. Na matéria, João destaca os desafios do setor da cotonicultura em meio aos recordes de crescimento.

Publicada em setembro deste ano, a reportagem concorria na categoria Internet. O jornalista recebeu, além da gratificação em dinheiro, um troféu.

🏆 É a terceira vez que João Souza ganha esse prêmio . No ano de 2025, o repórter, ao lado de Malu Vieira, levou a premiação na categoria internet com a reportagem "Tecnologia permite que cliente faça 'raio-x' de roupas e descubra em quais peças o algodão da Bahia foi transformado; entenda" .

Já em 2024, o repórter, também acompanhado de Malu, conquistou a mesma categoria com a reportagem "Pesquisadores debatem efeitos das mudanças climáticas no oeste da Bahia, 2ª maior produtora de algodão do Brasil" .

O prêmio acontece desde em 2019, quando foi lançado pela Associação Baiana dos Produtores de Algodão (Abapa). A iniciativa tem o objetivo de atrair o interesse das mídias local, regional e nacional para a produção de conteúdos sobre a cotonicultura baiana.

Além da categoria Internet, também podem vencer reportagens profissionais de TV e rádio, além de premiar estudantes.

articles.title: Cyberattacks threaten to make open source AI a little less open, Hugging Face exec warns  | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Hugging Face executive Irene Solaiman warns that growing cyberattacks on open AI platforms could force tighter security restrictions, threatening the accessibility that makes open source communities valuable to developers worldwide.
articles.body:
The very qualities that make open AI platforms valuable, like open doors and rich data, might also make them vulnerable to more hacks, Irene Solaiman, chief policy officer and SVP of strategy at Hugging Face, said on a recent episode of the Equity podcast .

The October attack on OpenCode , which targeted users’ third-party API keys and caused financial damage, is the latest example. It follows an incident this summer in which an OpenAI agent swarm breached Hugging Face in an apparent attempt to cover its tracks after accessing answers to cybersecurity evaluations.

The risks aren’t limited to platforms that invite open community contributions. On Monday, AI infrastructure startup Fireworks, which helps developers run and train open AI models, disclosed that attackers had accessed some customers’ model weights, datasets, and billing information. The company temporarily disabled certain self-service dataset functions as it investigates. While the attack isn’t necessarily due to Fireworks’ openness, it highlights how much valuable information is concentrated within AI infrastructure providers.

“The things I worry about making an open community targeted are also what makes it special,” Solaiman said on Equity. “We are necessarily permissive. We want the average hobbyist in their basement who doesn’t have an institutional affiliation to be able to contribute.”

“You want people to be able to just submit pull requests and allow anybody without a valid affiliation to contribute … but then you have some losers who ruin it for the rest,” she added in a separate conversation.

That permissiveness isn’t the only thing drawing attackers. The wealth of information open platforms host also makes them targets. Hugging Face became a temptation for OpenAI’s agent swarm because of the evaluation datasets it holds, whereas OpenCode’s target in this case came from its “juicy third-party API keys,” per Solaiman.

“The combination of that makes us prime targets,” Solaiman told TechCrunch in a separate conversation. She added that there’s a “danger of open source really closing down at a time when we’ve gotten so much public support.”

Much of the industry has come out recently in support of open AI models , including heavy hitters like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. And increasingly, governments, enterprises, and startups are relying on open models to build.

So what would a pullback actually look like? It could theoretically mean restrictions on who can upload models or datasets, more stringent identity verification, or additional vetting of developers before they can access certain features. While these moves could protect platforms from attackers, it could also make it more difficult for independent researchers and hobbyists to participate in communities they would have been welcomed in before.

For now, Hugging Face is trying to avoid that route. Solaiman said the company has been beefing up monitoring tools to catch hacks, as well as taking steps to prevent them. But monitoring can be expensive to maintain, she noted, and not every platform will be able to afford it.

“Administrative access tokens were part of what gave that agent swarm better access, so we just rotate them a lot more frequently than we used to,” Solaiman said. “We also now have stricter network controls.”

In other words, the credentials that give admins broad access to Hugging Face’s systems now get changed more often, which means a stolen token would be useful for less time.

Other parts of the open source ecosystem are dealing with similar security-related trade-offs. GitHub, the world’s largest host for open source projects, has been fighting off attackers who inject malicious code into projects to quickly spread malware. The company began tightening security requirements for publishing packages to the npm registry, revoking older authentication tokens, and limiting how long new ones remain valid.

Zach Steindler, an engineer at GitHub who handles software supply chain security, told TechCrunch via email that while security measures can disrupt established workflows, the platforms can become more secure without fundamentally restricting participation.

“It’s less about limiting functionality and more about going and fixing things that weren’t secure in the first place,” Steindler said. He noted that npm install scripts have existed for years, but recent attacks highlighted how dangerous they could be. GitHub worked with OpenJS — a nonprofit that hosts critical open source projects built with JavaScript — on a safer approach.

The same logic applies to where security teams put their effort, per Steindler: “Security is all about maximizing impact with the resources we have, and I would much rather invest in detecting suspicious behavior and containment capabilities: things that cover all accounts and access methods. Suspicious behavior is suspicious regardless of who is exhibiting it.”

articles.title: After a summer of reorganizing national debt, the Treasury borrowed more than $100 billion a week in October
articles.summary: The October 2026 deficit was $125 billion more than the shortfall recorded last October, the CBO reported.
articles.body:
The fiscal year of 2027 is not off to a great start for the U.S. Treasury's pocket book.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) just released its October budget report , the first month of the 2027 fiscal calendar year.

The strictly nonpartisan CBO reported that in October 2026, it estimated the federal government incurred a deficit of $409 billion—more than $100 billion a week. This is $125 billion more than the shortfall recorded last October.

Revenues were $36 billion lower, and outlays were $89 billion higher than the same month last year, according to the CBO. The report suggested October's federal deficit was that much higher due to shifts in the timing of certain federal payments that otherwise would have been made on November 1 (that date fell on a weekend in 2025 and 2026, therefore pushing those payments into October of each year).

This comes after a summer of debt reshuffling in the U.S. Treasury, with fiscal hawks questioning whether Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was moving deckchairs on the Titanic, rather than meaningfully improving the macroeconomic picture.

Bessent described this summer's actions as a "Treasury twist," a reference to policymaker action in which longer-dated Treasuries are bought and paid for by issuing shorter-term debt. The strategy has not been confirmed verbatim by the Treasury, but Bessent himself has indicated the scheme worked by buying back more expensive, long-term debt (in which yields, and hence interest, are higher) in lieu of cheaper, short-term debt.

The move did not impress markets. JPMorgan's co-head of global fundamental research, James Sullivan, described it as "paying your mortgage with your credit card. It can work for a while, but eventually the mismatch starts to become more obvious."

Context has since achieved the desired effect: A range of factors (including tough Fed talk on inflation and the recent AI rout) have brought down longer-dated yields and smoothed volatility.

While this has made government borrowing relatively cheaper in the long term (interest rates are tied to long-dated Treasury yields), it will do little to reassure debt hawks the U.S. fiscal trajectory is on a sustainable path.

In its budget review, the CBO showed that for the fiscal year of 2026, the deficit was at 6.2% of the nation's GDP, up from 5.8% a year prior. This percentage is greater than the 50-year average of 3.8%, and has only previously been matched or exceeded eight times since 1946: from 2009 through 2012 and in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.

articles.title: Hegseth on Vance’s criticism of the Iran war: ‘Politics is not really my thing’
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a Tuesday morning press conference deflected Vice President Vance’s earlier criticism that the Iran war led to stunning Republican losses in the midterm elections, telling reporters he respects Vance “greatly” but was “not going to exchange any finger-pointing.” “Thankfully, politics is not really my thing. I do the Department of…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a Tuesday morning press conference deflected Vice President Vance’s earlier criticism that the Iran war led to stunning Republican losses in the midterm elections, telling reporters he respects Vance “greatly” but was “not going to exchange any finger-pointing.”

“Thankfully, politics is not really my thing. I do the Department of War and making sure we’re prepared and ready. So a lot of people are going to look at the conflict and assess it,” Hegseth said.

He praised Vance as “a critical member of the team in every aspect of this” and said he was grateful for input the vice president has given the Pentagon chief personally.

But Hegseth added he agreed with President Trump when he said he would start the Iran war all over again, even if it is deeply unpopular.

“It was done for the right reasons to ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon,” he said. “As Marco Rubio said, I think quite well, it’s not necessarily popular, but it may have been necessary, and that’s certainly how I feel. It was a necessary undertaking.”

Hegseth has remained defiant in the face of impeachment proceedings against him in the House over the Iran war and other conflicts, calling the effort “a farce” and “a stunt.”

Hegseth’s first press briefing at the Pentagon in 189 days came after Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) on Monday unveiled eight articles of impeachment against him. Massie has accused the Defense chief of violating the Constitution and other laws during U.S. military operations in Iran, Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean.

Without mentioning Massie by name, Hegseth called him “one disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is following “a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” and he said Massie is attempting to “do damage to this president, this country, and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it” in his final days in Congress.

“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said. “In the 250 years of our American republic, no secretary of war or secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations, and in our case, successful ones at that.”

Hegseth also sought to tie himself to the president, comparing the impeachment effort against him to similar attempts to remove Trump from office in his first term — once over an alleged quid pro quo phone call with Ukraine and the second time over the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection at the Capitol.

“We’ve seen this show before. They impeached President Trump over a perfect phone call. They impeached him again in his final week in office. Both times they failed. Both times he came back stronger, and the American people sent him back to the White House,” Hegseth said.

“Now they’re trying a third time, this time against a member of his Cabinet. They will fail again, and if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.”

The speech appeared to please Trump, who shortly posted his review of the Pentagon chief to social media.

“Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Tuesday.

House lawmakers later Tuesday are expected to move on a key procedural step in the effort to impeach Hegseth, a first step that will determine whether the full lower chamber will move ahead on the eight impeachment articles.

articles.title: Majority of Republicans want Congress to end Iran war: Poll
articles.summary: A majority of Republicans in a recent survey said they want Congress to end the Iran war, which has stretched into its eighth month and increased gas and grocery prices. The Reuters/Ipsos poll, released Tuesday, found that 71 percent of respondents support legislation to end the Middle East conflict. This included 93 percent of Democrats…
articles.body:
A majority of Republicans in a recent survey said they want Congress to end the Iran war, which has stretched into its eighth month and increased gas and grocery prices .

The Reuters/Ipsos poll , released Tuesday, found that 71 percent of respondents support legislation to end the Middle East conflict. This included 93 percent of Democrats and 51 percent of Republicans.

President Trump’s approval rating for managing the Iran war has dipped to 26 percent. Another 62 percent of respondents disapproved of his policies around the conflict, 10 percent didn’t know and 2 percent skipped the question, the survey shows.

Among Democrats, 5 percent backed the president on the issue and 92 percent didn’t, while the remainder said they were unsure or skipped the question. For Republicans, 59 percent supported Trump on the Iran war, 31 percent did not, 9 percent did not know and less than half a percent skipped the question, according to the poll.

Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, attributed the rising unpopularity of the war to his October estimations , which found that it has cost American households $2,000 so far.

“Consider that the war’s costs taken together have absorbed about half the average American household’s income gain over the past eight months,” Zandi wrote on the social platform X . “No wonder the war is so unpopular.”

The conflict has cost the country at least $47 billion , while causing energy prices to skyrocket.

Congressional Democrats have listed ending the war as a top priority following the midterm election , which will give the party majorities in both the House and Senate next year.

“We are going to end the war. We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said at a press conference last week.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, has partnered with outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) on multiple failed Iran war powers resolutions . Khanna has also floated the idea of reintroducing further blocks to the war effort, including cutting off funding.

Trump over the weekend said the U.S. military was “unlikely” to renew attacks on Tehran as negotiations continue .

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted Nov. 6-9 among 1,705 respondents. The margin of error is 2.4 percentage points for all respondents.

articles.title: Blunt Rochester backs Democratic legislative push in face of Trump’s veto threat
articles.summary: While Democrats will have to contend with President Trump’s threats to veto legislation when they take control of Congress in January, Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) on Tuesday argued that reality should not be a deterrent to passing legislative priorities. Speaking at The Hill’s Health Next Summit in Washington, Blunt Rochester touched on healthcare priorities…
articles.body:
While Democrats will have to contend with President Trump’s threats to veto legislation when they take control of Congress in January, Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) on Tuesday argued that reality should not be a deterrent to passing legislative priorities.

Speaking at The Hill’s Health Next Summit in Washington, Blunt Rochester touched on healthcare priorities Democrats are eyeing as they prepare to control both the House and Senate.

She alluded to reinstating the enhanced Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits and reversing reductions in regulatory oversight that have occurred under the current administration.

NewsNation’s Washington Bureau Chief Mike Viqueira noted the reality that despite Democrats wresting back control over Congress in the midterms, Trump retains his veto power to halt any bills that may be passed.

“That shouldn’t stop us from putting forward what the American people said they wanted and what they voted for,” Blunt Rochester responded at the event, sponsored by AstraZeneca, the Healthcare Distribution Alliance and the Partnership to Advance Cardiovascular Health.

“I think you know there’s two tracks that we have to go down. One is to reverse those cuts. People haven’t even seen the impacts of the Medicaid cuts yet. They are coming,” she added, referring to the Medicaid rule changes scheduled to go into effect beginning on Jan. 1, such as new work requirements included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

“You’ve got the ACA tax credits, the Medicaid cuts, the impact that’s going to have on people with disabilities. The families have come to us and said this is a big concern for them, and then you’ve got to reverse and reimagine. The current system is not working for people,” Blunt Rochester said.

Trump has repeatedly threatened to heavily exercise his veto powers before and after it became clear that Democrats would retake Congress. But healthcare was a top concern in the midterms and he may bow to public pressure if Democrats manage to pass bipartisan healthcare legislation.

Polling from KFF showed that voters picked Democrats because they believed the party was better equipped at handling issues like healthcare access.

“In this moment, healthcare was on the ballot, and it is really one of the major issues that we’re going to have to tackle as we go into the 120th Congress,” Blunt Rochester, who sits on the Senate Health Committee, said.

images.caption: Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) in conversation with Mike Viqueira, Washington Bureau Chief at NewsNation, at during The Hill’s Health Next Summit at the Ronald Reagan Building and International Trade Center in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, November 10, 2026.

articles.title: Former GOP lawmaker, surgeon general say ‘transactional’ Trump might not veto bipartisan health legislation
articles.summary: Former Republican Rep. Larry Bucshon (Ind.) and former Surgeon General Jerome Adams both believe President Trump may hold off on vetoing any bipartisan healthcare legislation passed by a Democratic-controlled Congress, saying on Tuesday that Trump’s “transactional” nature and the final two years of his time in office could sway his decisions. At The Hill’s Health…
articles.body:
Former Republican Rep. Larry Bucshon (Ind.) and former Surgeon General Jerome Adams both believe President Trump may hold off on vetoing any bipartisan healthcare legislation passed by a Democratic-controlled Congress, saying on Tuesday that Trump’s “transactional” nature and the final two years of his time in office could sway his decisions.

At The Hill’s Health Next Summit , both Bucshon and Adams were asked whether they believed Trump would veto potential bipartisan healthcare legislation that lands on his desk.

“I think he might,” said Bucshon of the possibility Trump might sign such bipartisan legislation. “I think that the president historically is transactional. He’s in the last two years of what he’ll consider potential legacy for his presidency, particularly on a couple of issues: healthcare, immigration and a few others. So, I think if you get a good bipartisan legislation that the American people support, the president will sign it.”

Trump had threatened he would become “ Mr. Veto ” if Democrats took back control of Congress. When it became evident on Election Night that Democrats had won both the House and Senate, Trump posted a photo of a hat on Truth Social emblazoned with the word “VETO.”

Despite these signals from Trump, Adams agreed with Bucshon, saying he wasn’t convinced the president would exercise this power as readily as he indicated.

Noting his recent interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes,” Adams said Trump was aware that the country was “frustrated” with him.

“The question actually is: Will this current iteration of Congress be able to come together and put forward bipartisan legislation on healthcare?” Adams said at the event, which was sponsored by AstraZeneca, the Healthcare Distribution Alliance and the Partnership to Advance Cardiovascular Health.

“I think that if they can; if the Democrats can come together amongst themselves. Number one, because you’ve got two different factions of the Democratic Party who have very different ideas about what healthcare legislation should look like, and in turn they can bring along Republicans, and they actually pass bipartisan legislation, I feel very confident that we have a good chance of it not getting vetoed because it would clearly then be defying the will of the American people,” he added.

Democrats are compiling their list of legislative priorities for when they take control in January, and chief among their health goals is restoring the enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits.

When Congress was negotiating renewing the credits last year, more than a dozen Republicans voted alongside Democrats on legislation to save them. Now, with Democrats poised to hold solid majorities in the House and Senate, the chances of a bipartisan agreement being reached have risen exponentially.

Before that can occur, however, former Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Director Mandy Cohen warned on Tuesday that the healthcare affordability crisis will get worse before it improves.

“First, affordability is going to get worse. I think everyone should understand it’s going to get worse before it gets better,” Cohen said at the Health Next Summit.

“When you take billions of dollars out of the healthcare system, that goes somewhere. You squeeze the balloon one place, it comes out and employers are feeling that right now,” she added. “When you destabilize the individual market, like we did when we took away subsidies, coming out of employers, right? And that means wages get depressed. But also, AI; I’m a fan of what it could potentially accomplish. Right now, it’s just jacking up the cost of healthcare.”

articles.title: Jeffries pushes tighter China chip restrictions amid Nvidia CEO scandal
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) backed an effort Monday to pass new restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips through an annual defense bill amid a scandal over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Jeffries, who could become Speaker in the next Congress, said he “strongly supports” chip restrictions…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) backed an effort Monday to pass new restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips through an annual defense bill amid a scandal over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Jeffries, who could become Speaker in the next Congress, said he “strongly supports” chip restrictions in the Senate’s version of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

“We’re going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version,” he told reporters at the Capitol on Monday.

The Senate version of the NDAA currently includes three chip export bills — the Artificial Intelligence Oversight of Verified Exports and Restrictions on Weaponizable Advanced Technology to Covered High-Risk Actors Act, the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act and the Chip Security Act.

The bills would allow Congress to block advanced AI chip exports to U.S. foreign adversaries, bar the sale of essential chipmaking tools to countries of concern and require restricted AI chips to have a “location verification mechanism” to ensure they aren’t improperly diverted.

They are gaining new momentum after the Nvidia CEO disclosed over the weekend that he had an affair with a woman who U.S. officials concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The company’s chips are central to the AI boom, powering the technology’s development. As some of the most advanced products on the market, they have often been the focus of U.S. export controls.

Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday it was launching an investigation, with a focus on the U.S. national and economic security implications of the incident.

Jeffries and several other lawmakers met Monday in the Capitol for a classified briefing with several top administration officials, including Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, and CIA Director John Ratcliffe.

While the conversation was primarily focused on Iran, the topic of Nvidia came up, Jeffries noted, saying it’s clear there are “real concerns that need to be addressed.”

“What is clear, and the Nvidia issue did come up, [is] that we’re going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of America’s national security,” he added.

articles.title: Average cost of gas drops to less than $4 per gallon for first time since July
articles.summary: The national average for the cost of gas dropped to less than $4 per gallon on Tuesday for the first time since July, as prices soared in the months following the start of the Iran war. According to AAA, the average price of gas hit $3.98 per gallon, the first time in 114 days that…
articles.body:
The national average for the cost of gas dropped to less than $4 per gallon on Tuesday for the first time since July, as prices soared in the months following the start of the Iran war.

According to AAA , the average price of gas hit $3.98 per gallon, the first time in 114 days that the fuel was priced at less than $4 a gallon. Several states still have high energy prices, with most of the Northeast, excluding Rhode Island, and much of the western U.S. still seeing prices of more than $4.

Nevada, California and Hawaii have average prices close to $6 a gallon, while most of the South has seen the cost sink to less than $3.70 per gallon, AAA’s website states.

This decline came as oil futures dipped 13 percent last week, when the global crude oil benchmark Brent saw its biggest drop since April 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Oil prices fell another 5 percent on Monday to their lowest level since Aug. 31, reaching just less than $90 a barrel Tuesday.

After President Trump said last week that he did not have a plan to renew attacks on Iran and Democrats notched sweeping victories in last week’s midterm elections , markets bet that Democratic control of Congress would cap Trump’s economically disruptive policies, including the conflict, NBC News reported.

Iran’s effective shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz following the start of the war on Feb. 28 has caused gas prices to skyrocket. The ensuing energy shortage was the result of Tehran closing the key waterway, where roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil is exported.

The conflict has been widely unpopular among the American public, with Trump, Vice President Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and other administration officials acknowledging that it likely led to Republican defeats last week.

The president on Monday downplayed the likelihood of renewed strikes on the Iranian regime after meeting with the primary interlocutor with Iran, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.

“Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding that the U.S. naval and land blockades amount to a “status quo.”

Trump also noted that the conflict was “ending quickly, but we want to take care of people that have been very good to us over the years,” referring to partners in the region like Qatar.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday gave the U.S. an ultimatum after Tehran submitted a two-day proposal to end the conflict or “choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”

This came as the U.S. reportedly launched defensive strikes against Iran shortly before and after the midterms .

In a new filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Anthropic said it is planning to sell 825 million shares between $70 and $78 a share. If the company lists shares at the…
articles.body:
Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for its blockbuster initial public offering (IPO) expected later this month.

In a new filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Anthropic said it is planning to sell 825 million shares between $70 and $78 a share. If the company lists shares at the top of the range, on a fully diluted basis, it would put the company’s total valuation at around $1.4 trillion, a jump from the $965 billion valuation the company hit last May.

Shares will be offered under the ticket “ANT.”

The Claude maker is expected to go public later this month, despite lingering questions around a volatile market in the wake of AI concerns.

Stocks initially soared one day after Democrats won elections to control the Senate and House.

This was followed by a drastic sell-off last Thursday. Incumbent lawmakers and candidates campaigned on reining in the AI industry, while voters rejected data centers on dozens of ballot measures across the country.

Anthropic publicly filed for its IPO late last month and is likely to become the first large frontier AI lab to go public.

Its S-1 filing last month showed Anthropic’s revenue has drastically jumped in the past year, yet the company reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of this year.

AI safety concerns have dominated headlines for months , following various security breaches and warnings from executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, about the technology’s risks to society .

Anthropic highlighted various risks of the technology in last month’s S-1, including the potential for cyberattacks, design of biological weapons or mass surveillance by governments.

“We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level,” the company wrote.

Anthropic confidentially filed paperwork with the SEC in early June, though no other details were released at the time. A week later, rival AI company OpenAI also confidentially filed to go public , though it is not clear when the ChatGPT maker will take the next step.

There was speculation Anthropic could beat the IPO record recently set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX last June, in which shares opened at $150.

articles.title: N-able takes its remote access service offline after researcher publishes dozens of zero-day bugs | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The remote access giant also urged its self-hosted customers to take down their own servers amid a "critical security incident," fearing the possibility of cyberattacks.
articles.body:
Remote access company N-able has confirmed it took down its cloud-hosted offering to fix a slew of security vulnerabilities that were published online this week, giving the company no advance notice to fix them.

In a status update on its website, the company said its hosted N-Central offering for customers is now offline “while we take the necessary actions to secure the environments and implement appropriate remediation.” The company also urged customers to take down their own self-hosted deployments of N-Central, fearing that attackers could use the publicly disclosed exploits to hack into customer networks.

N-able said during this time customers will not be able to use their N-Central service, which allows corporate customers to remotely access and manage other devices and systems on the same network. Remote access technologies are a frequent target of hackers, as these systems can grant vast access to a company’s network and internal data.

Security researcher Ben Bales released the “zero-day” bugs on GitHub on Sunday. In a post on X , Bales dubbed the bugs Able2Shell, describing them as a mix of vulnerabilities capable of stealing credentials, creating new administrative accounts, and gaining root access to affected N-able systems.

Bales told Bleeping Computer that he publicly released the bugs as the company allegedly failed to patch the flaws reported in a different product.

N-able said that it has no evidence of successful exploitation against any of its customer environments. A spokesperson for the company did not respond to a request for comment about whether it has the ability to check, such as server logs, or if it has no way to check.

articles.title: Investigators recover voice recorder from a jet crash in Florida that killed 9
articles.summary: Investigators said Monday they have recovered the cockpit voice recorder from a business jet that plummeted from the sky amid severe weather in Florida last week, killing all nine people on board.
articles.body:
(AP) — Investigators said Monday they have recovered the cockpit voice recorder from a business jet that plummeted from the sky amid severe weather in Florida last week, killing all nine people on board.

The recorder was found at the site where the Bahamas-bound Learjet slammed into the ground and erupted in a fireball Nov. 1, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said in a statement posted to social media.

If data from the device can be recovered, it could provide crucial details about what the pilots said to each other as they encountered turbulence, ice formed on the wings and they lost control of the aircraft.

It was not immediately known if the recorder had been damaged or if it was working in the first place. The NTSB said the device was being evaluated at a lab in Washington.

From photos the agency posted online, showing the recorder’s orange-painted metal shell, it appeared to be in decent shape, aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti told The Associated Press.

“It’s very plausible that any info on the recorder survived,” Guzzetti said. “If they can recover it, and it’s from the accident flight, that will be a huge help to investigators.”

He noted that when the NTSB recovered the cockpit voice recorder from a medical transport plane that crashed in Philadelphia in January 2025, killing seven people, it turned out the device likely had not been functioning for several years.

Witnesses captured dramatic video as the business jet plunged nose-first into the ground, and air traffic control transmissions recorded the disturbing moments as the pilots realized their fate. But the cockpit voice recorder could shed light on other aspects of the crash, including why the Learjet appeared to steer around a large storm cell only to head directly into a rapidly developing smaller one.

Investigators have said pieces of a key part of the tail called the elevator, which controls the plane’s pitch, were found more than a mile away from the main crater, confirming the plane started to break apart before impact.

The co-pilot told air traffic controllers that the plane was being thrown up and down more than 700 feet (213 meters), and she asked them for a better route through the area.

Generally, it takes 12 to 18 months for the NTSB to complete a crash investigation, but complicated cases can take longer. The NTSB’s roughly 400 workers are pursuing more than 1,200 active investigations.

Investigators will review maintenance records and any history of problems with the plane. They will also interview officials at Upper Jets, the company that operated the flight, as well as air traffic controllers and people who work at the airport in Austin, Texas, from where the plane departed.

articles.title: Trump administration disburses $10 billion in rural healthcare funds
articles.summary: The Trump administration announced Monday that it is going to roll out $10 billion to 50 states in its second installment of the $50 billion rural healthcare fund which was created as part of the administration’s One Big Beautiful Act last year. “President Trump made a historic investment in rural America, and HHS is putting…
articles.body:
The Trump administration announced Monday that it is going to roll out $10 billion to 50 states in its second installment of the $50 billion rural healthcare fund which was created as part of the administration’s One Big Beautiful Act last year.

“President Trump made a historic investment in rural America, and HHS is putting those resources to work in every state,” said Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr in a press release on Monday.

“This next $10 billion will expand access to care, strengthen the rural health workforce, improve prevention, and help states build solutions that fit the needs of their own communities. We are giving rural America the resources and flexibility to build stronger health systems that deliver better care and better outcomes,” he continued.

With the second year of funding, the administration will left with $30 billion in funds which are expected to be rolled out to states on a yearly basis until 2030. The funds are meant to improve healthcare access, quality and outcomes in rural communities across the nation, according to a fact sheet from the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS).

All participating states receive a baseline funding of $100 million each year which makes up about half of the annual funding of the Rural Health Transformation Program, while the other half is allocated based on factors such as the state’s rural population, initiatives in the state’s rural health transformation plan and policy actions, according to the fact sheet.

“Rural Americans have life expectancies three years shorter than their urban peers, but President Trump’s Rural Health Transformation Program is funding the historic investments necessary to close that gap,” said CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz in the release .

“States have already put these resources to work bringing better care closer to home for their rural communities, and CMS looks forward to helping them build on that progress in the coming year,” Oz added.

Some states will receive a higher amount of funds as compared to others in the second installment with Texas and Alaska being at the top of the chart with over $280 million and $270 million in allocated funds, according to the release.

The five-year-funding of $50 billion is less than the estimated cuts of federal Medicaid spending in rural areas which adds up to $137 billion over a course of ten years, according to an analysis by independent health policy research organization KFF .

This announcement comes after the Democrats won a stunning victory in the midterm elections, taking control of both the House and the Senate. Democratic candidates made healthcare affordability a central focus in their campaigns leading up to the election.

Recent polling conducted before the midterms showed over half the respondents backed Democrats’ performance over Republicans in terms of healthcare.

articles.title: Hot inflation report has Wall Street eyeing whether the Fed could make a jumbo rate hike next month
articles.summary: A hotter-than-expected October inflation reading showed that inflation remained elevated after soaring in September, solidifying the odds of a Federal Reserv...
articles.body:
A hotter-than-expected October inflation reading showed that inflation remains elevated after soaring in September, solidifying the odds the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month.

It's even raising the specter of a jumbo half-percentage-point hike.

The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October, compared with expectations of 0.3%, marking a slight cooldown from September's 0.6% gain. "Core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, compared with expectations of 0.2% and unchanged from September.

The Labor Department did not report a 12-month inflation rate for October — the measure of how much prices climbed over the past year — because of last fall's government shutdown. Prices in October 2025 were never measured.

"The stronger-than-expected 0.3% rise in the core CPI in October was similar to September's in that it was very broad-based, rather than driven by any one-off or temporary factors," said Thomas Ryan, economist for Capital Economics. "This should all but confirm a December hike, with the strength of inflationary pressures in the last two months raising the risk that the Fed opts for a larger 50bp move rather than 25bp."

Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede, looks at two specific data points to assess whether inflation is returning to target, and both moved the wrong way in October.

Services minus the cost of housing rose 0.5%, the highest reading since May, extending the sticky services dynamic that has been the central obstacle to getting price trends back to 2% all year. Pride said that measure needs to average out near 0.2% before there is a credible case that broad inflation is falling to the Fed's 2% target. Meanwhile, goods prices excluding food, energy, and used cars rose 0.4%, the highest since January.

Given these trends, Pride warned that investors should plan for rates at or above today's level well into next year, with the path beyond December dependent on whether services prices finally turn.

The immediate question is the size of the Fed's next move.

"Will the central bank deliver a 25 basis points or 50 basis points move?" said James McCann, senior economist at Edward Jones, noting that price growth was again stronger than feared.

"We think it is most likely that the Fed will deliver a 25 basis points move, especially with oil prices moving lower in recent days and financial conditions increasingly volatile," he said. "However, the risk of a bigger 50 basis points move cannot be ruled out."

articles.title: Exxon moves toward return to Venezuela
articles.summary: Oil giant ExxonMobil has taken a major step toward returning to Venezuela to produce oil. The firm has signed a memorandum of understanding with the South American nation to evaluate opportunities for drilling there. “We welcome the opportunity to evaluate potential upstream opportunities with the Venezuelan government and PDVSA,” said a spokesperson for the firm,…
articles.body:
Oil giant ExxonMobil has taken a major step toward returning to Venezuela to produce oil.

The firm has signed a memorandum of understanding with the South American nation to evaluate opportunities for drilling there.

“We welcome the opportunity to evaluate potential upstream opportunities with the Venezuelan government and PDVSA,” said a spokesperson for the firm, referring to Venezuela’s state-run oil company Petróleos de Venezuela.

“This memorandum is a meaningful first step, but any future investment would require stable policies, clear regulations, strong investment protections and competitive returns,” the spokesperson added, not providing any additional details.

While the memo appears to stop short of a full commitment, it comes after Exxon CEO Darren Woods called Venezuela “uninvestable” under current conditions earlier this year.

President Trump, meanwhile, has sought to push U.S. companies to invest in the Latin American nation’s oil after the U.S. invasion at the start of the year.

“We’re going to have our very large United States oil companies, the biggest anywhere in the world, go in, spend billions of dollars, fix the badly broken infrastructure, the oil infrastructure, and start making money for the country,” he said in January after capturing the nation’s leader, Nicolás Maduro.

Around that time, the Trump administration indicated it would be in control of Venezuela’s oil, with Energy Secretary Chris Wright saying the U.S. would sell the petroleum “indefinitely.”

Since that time, the U.S. has struck up its own Venezuelan oil partnership with private operator North American Blue Energy Partners.

Exxon left Venezuela in 2007 amid a nationalization push by then-President Hugo Chávez.

Chevron remained in Venezuela and recently announced plans to double its production there.

Venezuela is estimated to have massive quantities of oil under its surface .

Trump’s war in Iran, meanwhile, has driven up global oil prices by constraining supplies out of the Middle East, raising gasoline prices along with it.

As of Tuesday, the average U.S. gas price was about $3.98 per gallon according to AAA , dropping below $4 for the first time in months , but it still is about 91 cents higher than at this time last year.

While oil prices have fallen in recent days, new investments in Venezuela are unlikely to immediately move the needle on oil or gasoline prices because it could take significant time to get any additional production underway.

articles.title: Is AI deciding who's dangerous in Michigan prisons?
articles.summary: Michigan's new prison scoring system claims 30% better violence prediction, but Recidiviz says it doesn't actually use AI to classify inmates.
articles.body: What if a computer-generated score could influence whether someone lives in a low-security prison dorm or a tightly controlled cell? Michigan is preparing to test new technology that could affect exactly that. State officials say the system could improve predictions of future prison violence by approximately 30%. That's a big claim, especially when the safety of correctional officers and incarcerated people could depend on getting those assessments right. But there's something important missing from early reports about Michigan prison AI. Despite headlines suggesting artificial intelligence will determine how dangerous someone might be, the nonprofit developing the software says AI plays no role in calculating security scores. Instead, the technology follows predetermined rules, and corrections staff make the final decisions. So, how does the system work? And can Michigan really predict prison violence more accurately without putting too much trust in a computer-generated score? FEDERAL INMATES MAY SOON GET TABLETS WITH MESSAGING CAPABILITIES AS BUREAU OF PRISONS MAKES MODERNIZATION PUSH Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. Why security levels can change life behind bars The Michigan Department of Corrections oversees approximately 32,000 incarcerated people statewide. Currently, corrections employees use a manual scoring process to determine the appropriate security level for each person. Those classifications influence where someone lives and how closely they're supervised. They can also affect access to educational programs and job training opportunities. For someone serving a lengthy sentence, a change in security level can make a significant difference in daily life. Michigan has four general population security levels: I, II, IV and V. Level I generally allows greater freedom of movement, while Level V involves much tighter supervision. People at lower security levels may have access to more vocational training and higher education opportunities. However, Michigan says programs such as Violence Prevention Programming remain available at every general population security level. There is no general population Level III. Now, the state wants a better way to determine which security level fits each person's current behavior and needs. What Michigan's new scoring system will change The Michigan Department of Corrections plans to begin testing the new system on Dec. 1 at selected men's prisons. If the pilot performs well, officials could eventually expand the technology to additional facilities. One significant change involves how often corrections staff can reassess someone's security level. Instead of relying on information collected at scheduled intervals, the new system will allow ongoing reviews using updated prison records. That could help staff recognize changes in behavior sooner. The software comes from Recidiviz, a nonprofit technology organization that supports criminal justice agencies in 19 states. Its team analyzed 10 years of Michigan prison classification data to help redesign the state's scoring process. Here's how it works. The software examines information already in prison records and calculates a score using factors selected by Michigan corrections experts. Recent disciplinary incidents may carry more weight than incidents from years ago. Meanwhile, someone who maintains good behavior over time may have an opportunity to qualify for a lower security level. Completing certain rehabilitation programs can also help someone qualify for a less restrictive classification. Additionally, the software can flag a person's record when new information warrants another review. Michigan Department of Corrections Director Heidi E. Washington believes the changes could help improve safety. "Classifying prisoners at the security level that fits their current behaviors and needs keeps everyone safer," Washington said in the state's announcement. She also expressed optimism that the combination of historical information and research-based scoring could strengthen security throughout Michigan's prison system. The idea sounds promising. But how much confidence should officials place in those computer-generated scores? GRANDMOTHER SUES AFTER ALLEGED AI FACIAL RECOGNITION ERROR LED TO MONTHS IN JAIL, EXPERTS SOUND ALARM Is Michigan actually using AI to predict prison violence? This is where the story takes an unexpected turn. On Nov. 2, Recidiviz published an explanation titled, Why We Don't Use AI to Classify People in Prisons. The nonprofit confirmed that Michigan's new classification system does not use artificial intelligence to calculate security scores. The system relies on a points-based formula that corrections employees can examine. You may hear this type of formula called an algorithm. That's simply a set of instructions a computer follows to complete a task. Think of it like a digital scorecard. The computer reviews specific information and adds up the points according to established rules. Give it the same information, and it produces the same score. Recidiviz says Michigan corrections experts helped determine which factors belong in the scoring process. Staff can review the calculations and override a score when circumstances require it. For example, someone might have medical needs or personal safety concerns that call for a different housing assignment. Corrections employees can consider that information before making the final decision. Now, Recidiviz does use AI in other parts of its technology platform. Some tools help corrections employees prepare case notes and organize information from meetings. However, the organization says AI does not determine someone's security level or release. And here's what I find interesting. We're hearing about AI being used in nearly every industry. Yet this particular system relies on a more traditional approach to computer software. That clarification is important because people deserve to understand how technology influences decisions affecting someone's daily life. Still, using a rules-based system doesn't guarantee perfect results. Even straightforward software can produce questionable scores when the information behind its calculations contains errors. Can Michigan really predict prison violence 30% better? This is the number that really caught my attention. In its Oct. 28 announcement, the Michigan Department of Corrections said the redesigned system is expected to improve its ability to predict future violence by approximately 30%. That's a substantial improvement if the technology delivers it. However, the announcement doesn't explain how officials calculated that figure or provide the underlying performance results. For example, will the system identify more people who might become violent? Could it also incorrectly classify someone as dangerous? And how will officials know whether it's performing better than the current process? Those questions deserve answers because someone's security classification can affect their daily life throughout their sentence. There's another issue worth considering. The software depends on prison records. If a disciplinary report contains inaccurate information, that mistake could influence someone's score. Even when the information is correct, a risk assessment cannot predict with certainty what someone will do in the future. NORTHEASTERN CITY VOTES TO END SHOTSPOTTER CONTRACT FOR GUNFIRE-DETECTION TECH DESIGNED TO FIGHT CRIME Why better prison technology may not solve Michigan's biggest problem Even if Michigan's new software delivers more accurate security scores, officials still face a challenge that technology cannot solve on its own. What happens when someone needs higher-security housing but there's no appropriate bed available? Byron Osborn, president of the union representing Michigan corrections officers, raised that concern in recent reporting. According to Osborn, the department faces a shortage of higher-security beds. He argues that the bigger problem involves a lack of appropriate housing for people already classified as higher risk. Consider what happens if the software identifies someone who needs tighter supervision. Corrections staff agree with the assessment, but the prison lacks space in the appropriate security unit. Now what? The computer may have helped identify a potential safety concern. However, officials still need somewhere appropriate to house that person. Michigan has announced plans to add 870 high-security beds as part of its Safe Prisons Initiative. Some facility conversions are already underway, while larger construction projects will take longer to complete. More than 400 of those beds will come from two new high-security units at Oaks Correctional Facility and St. Louis Correctional Facility. The state expects those construction projects to take approximately two and a half years. Osborn has warned that corrections officers and incarcerated people need solutions sooner. Meanwhile, the state has experienced serious violence inside its prisons, including several recent incidents in which incarcerated people were suspected of killing their cellmates. Better classification could help officials recognize potentially dangerous situations sooner. But the department still needs sufficient staffing and appropriate housing to respond. And that raises another question. How much safer can a prison become if officials identify a problem but lack the resources to address it? Kurt's key takeaways I can see why Michigan wants to try something new. Nobody wants to see more violence inside prisons, and if technology can help prevent it, I'm all for giving it a chance. But I was surprised to learn that despite all the talk about AI, this new system actually uses a fairly straightforward scoring process. Corrections staff still make the final decisions, which I think is important when you're dealing with people's safety. Now, that 30% improvement Michigan is talking about sounds impressive. But I'd really like to know how they arrived at that number. And what happens when the computer gets someone's risk level wrong? Maybe a person has turned their life around, but an old disciplinary record still works against them. That's the kind of situation I'd want someone to take a closer look at before making a decision. There's also the bigger issue of whether Michigan has enough high-security beds and corrections officers to act on these assessments. You can have the best scoring system in the world, but what good does it do if there's nowhere appropriate to house someone who needs closer supervision? I'll be interested to see what happens when the pilot begins Dec. 1. If it leads to safer prisons and gives people a fairer way to demonstrate they've changed, that would be something worth talking about. But Michigan needs to show us the results. Would you trust a computer-generated score to help determine how dangerous someone might be, or should decisions affecting someone's safety remain entirely in human hands? articles.title: John Kerry says China now leads on green energy: ‘The rest of the world is stumbling along’
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State John Kerry warned in an interview published Tuesday the rest of the world is falling behind China when it comes to clean energy technology, arguing the country has emerged as the clear leader in a rapidly growing market. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the…
articles.body:
Former Secretary of State John Kerry warned in an interview published Tuesday the rest of the world is falling behind China when it comes to clean energy technology, arguing the country has emerged as the clear leader in a rapidly growing market.

“The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” Kerry, who worked under the second Obama administration, told The Guardian .

The warning comes as world leaders gather in Turkey for the COP31 United Nations Climate Summit, during which China’s growing influence over the clean energy industry has raised questions about whether it will assume a larger role in international climate negotiations.

China, the world’s largest greenhouse gas emitter, has also become the leading producer of clean energy technology. Its clean-tech exports exceeded $220 billion in 2025, and the country accounts for roughly 85 percent of global solar supply chain production as well as 80 percent of lithium-ion battery production capacity, according to the International Energy Agency.

Kerry, who also served as former President Biden’s special envoy for climate, argued finances — and not just environmental concerns — are pushing countries to find ways to transition away from fossil fuels.

“They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognize where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet and understand where costs are exorbitant and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said, referring to countries considering investments in clean energy.

“Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”

He also pointed to the ongoing war in Iran and shipping disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz as reasons countries are seeking to reduce their dependence on fuel imports.

“[China] reali z ed suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent,” Kerry said. “Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the S trait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently.”

articles.title: Tillis ‘leaning toward’ impeaching Hegseth if articles reach Senate
articles.summary: Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Tuesday he’s prepared to vote to oust Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should the House pass an impeachment resolution against the Pentagon chief this week, setting up the Senate for a full trial. “If it comes over, if there’s a vote, I’m likely to vote against Hegseth and for the…
articles.body:
Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Tuesday he’s prepared to vote to oust Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should the House pass an impeachment resolution against the Pentagon chief this week, setting up the Senate for a full trial.

“If it comes over, if there’s a vote, I’m likely to vote against Hegseth and for the impeachment,” Tillis told reporters on Capitol Hill.

“To me it’s a no-confidence vote for him. The best thing that we can do is move him along, get somebody in there that can help. Look, we’re struggling to get defense spending, and I lay that at his feet,” he added.

Tillis is one of at least six Senate Republicans who have entertained a full Senate trial for Hegseth after outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) announced eight articles of impeachment against him Monday.

Massie is forcing a vote this week to remove Hegseth under the articles, accusing the Defense secretary of abusing his powers with regards to several miliary operations throughout the second Trump administration, including the war in Iran, and strikes on suspected drug carrying boats around South America.

Hegseth responded in a news conference at the Pentagon Tuesday morning, calling Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” and the impeachment “a political spectacle.” Massie lost his primary to a Trump-backed challenger earlier this year.

Also keeping their minds open to a trial are GOP Sens. Bill Cassidy (La.), John Curtis (Utah), John Cornyn (Texas), John Boozman (Ark.) and Shelley Moore Capito (W.Va.).

House GOP leadership is working furiously behind the scenes to kill Massie’s push by burying the Hegseth resolution in committee vote Tuesday evening. But if it ultimately passes, a Senate trial would be the next step.

The White House also is reportedly working behind the scenes to call on loyalists in Congress to kill the resolution.

With Republicans controlling the House until January, Tuesday’s impeachment vote needs at least a few Republicans to vote with Democrats for the resolution to succeed.

articles.title: Fed's Bowman says inflation is broadening: 'There's more work to do' on rates
articles.summary: "Inflation pressures have persisted for longer than I had hoped," she said.
articles.body:
Federal Reserve governor Michelle Bowman said Tuesday that inflation is showing signs of broadening and suggested raising interest rates further to slow the pace of price increases.

"Inflation pressures have persisted for longer than I had hoped and have shown recent signs of broadening," Bowman said in a speech in Washington at the Council on Foreign Relations.

At the same time, she noted job market conditions appear to be firming.

"This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2%," she said.

She is also monitoring volatility in the markets to see how financial conditions influence the economic outlook.

Data released Tuesday revealed that inflation remained sticky in October. The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October , compared with expectations of 0.3%, marking a slight cooldown from September's 0.6% gain. "Core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, unchanged from September.

"The latest data suggest that these pressures may be broadening," said Bowman. "It is important to ensure that those inflationary pressures do not intensify, further broaden, or become embedded in consumer and business expectations.

"But today's Consumer Price Index data suggest that inflation pressures may persist for longer."

The hotter-than-expected report has Wall Street pricing in a rate hike next month as a done deal. The question is how big — 25 basis points or 50 basis points.

Looking at CPI, Bowman estimates that the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the core Personal Consumption Expenditures index — likely moved up to 3.3% in October from 3.1% in September on higher energy prices and the AI build-out that flowed to goods and services prices.

While she expects the effects of tariffs to wane and energy prices to come down when the Middle East conflict resolves, she said inflation from the AI build-out could persist.

"Monetary policy cannot offset the direct effects of tariffs and energy costs on inflation, but it plays a central role in containing the second-round effects," Bowman said.

Bowman raised the risk that if geopolitical tensions persist, energy prices may stay elevated in the near term, increasing the possibility that core inflation may also stay elevated because of increased pass-through to consumer prices.

She also sees a number of risks to the outlook for the economy, including a large correction in stock prices if returns on AI investment fall short of expectations, and a sharp increase in private long-term interest rates. Bowman noted lower stock prices could undermine the resilience seen in consumer spending.

articles.title: Democrats escalate probe of Trump admin drug pricing deals
articles.summary: Congressional Democrats are demanding pharmaceutical companies immediately disclose the un-redacted details of their “most favored nation” agreements with the Trump administration, according to a source familiar with the effort. The request to drugmakers comes from the potential health policy leaders in Congress next year — Democratic Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. (N.J.) of the Energy and…
articles.body:
Congressional Democrats are demanding pharmaceutical companies immediately disclose the un-redacted details of their “most favored nation” agreements with the Trump administration, according to a source familiar with the effort.

The request to drugmakers comes from the potential health policy leaders in Congress next year — Democratic Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. (N.J.) of the Energy and Commerce Committee, Richard Neal (Mass.) of the Ways and Means Committee and Bobby Scott (Va.) of the Education and Workforce Committee and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) of the Senate Finance Committee.

It represents a significant escalation of Democrats’ oversight and signals to pharmaceutical companies the new Democratic majority is going to scrutinize their dealings with the Trump administration.

If the companies can’t provide details of the agreements for some reason — such as potential non-disclosure agreements with the White House— they were told to meet with lawmakers in the next two weeks to discuss how they plan to fulfill the request, the source said.

The same four lawmakers sent a letter in March requesting copies of the most-favored-nation agreements, which the administration ignored. Once in power, Democrats will have the ability to demand documents, issue subpoenas and hold hearings on the Trump administration’s agenda.

Democrats have been skeptical of the administration’s drug pricing deals, which both Trump administration officials and company executives have said are confidential. Lawmakers want to know what the drug companies are getting in return for their agreements to lower prices for Medicaid.

Under the agreements, manufacturers have pledged not to charge more than the lowest international price for select products.

The deals have been a key part of the Trump administration’s health agenda, and lawmakers want verify claims Trump and other administration officials have been making about the savings the American people receive.

articles.title: Bond yields surge most in 19 months as traders brace for Fed rate hikes
articles.summary: US Treasuries slumped, pushing yields sharply higher, after hotter-than-expected inflation data and comments from a key Federal Reserve official fueled bets...
articles.body:
US Treasuries slumped, pushing yields sharply higher, after hotter-than-expected inflation data and comments from a key Federal Reserve official fueled bets that the central bank would need to deliver more aggressive interest rate hikes to cool inflation.

The two-year Treasury yield, which closely tracks expectations for Fed policy, surged 17 basis points on Tuesday. The two-year yield saw its biggest single-day jump since April 2025, when President Donald Trump's unveiling of tariffs rocked financial markets.

The rocky day for bonds started after Fed Governor Chris Waller said during remarks in London that he would consider backing a jumbo rate hike of 50 basis points (a half point) at the US central bank's December policy meeting if core inflation – a measure that strips out the volatile categories of food and energy – continues to come in at 0.3% or higher.

"Then, a stronger policy move may be needed," he said. "Hiking only 25 basis points [a quarter point] would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take."

Waller said he wants to monitor how the AI buildout is impacting prices of high-tech goods, and if the rise in energy prices this year is continuing to add to inflationary pressures. Oil prices have dropped in recent days, but remain well-above their pre-Iran war levels.

Consumer price data released Tuesday showed core inflation rose 0.3% from a month earlier, more than the 0.2% increase economists had expected. Yields surged higher after the data release.

The key 10-year Treasury yield jumped 10 basis points to 4.98% and briefly rose above 5% during trading. The 10-year yield influences the cost of borrowing across the economy, most notably mortgage rates.

An auction of 10-year notes on Tuesday saw soft demand, according to market strategist Peter Boockvar, adding to pressure on bonds.

Meanwhile, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said in remarks in Houston on Tuesday that the Fed needs to deliver at least two additional quarter-point rate increases.

"The exact pace of increases could depend on the near-term economic and financial environment," Logan said. "It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the [Fed] has moved so far this fall."

Traders are now pricing in a 91% chance of a quarter-point rate hike and a 9% chance of a half-point rate hike in December, according to CME FedWatch. Just one week ago, traders were pricing in a 77% chance of a quarter-point hike and a 23% chance of the Fed holding rates steady.

"October's economic data profile and a hawkish shift in Fed-speak have prompted the market to reassess whether a faster pace of Fed policy tightening may be warranted," Vail Hartman, US rates strategist at BMO Capital Markets, wrote in a note.

articles.title: Nvidia hires former acting US attorney to investigate Jensen Huang
articles.summary: Nvidia announced Tuesday that it has hired a former acting U.S. attorney to investigate its CEO, Jensen Huang, following reports of his alleged intimate relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe was spying for China. “The independent members of the NVIDIA Board have retained former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New…
articles.body:
Nvidia announced Tuesday that it has hired a former acting U.S. attorney to investigate its CEO, Jensen Huang, following reports of his alleged intimate relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe was spying for China.

“The independent members of the NVIDIA Board have retained former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a thorough and independent investigation as was announced on Sunday,” the company said in a statement Tuesday .

This comes after the company board announced Sunday that they would be initiating an independent investigation into the accusations stemming from a New York Times report that claimed American spy agencies discovered Alice Huang illegally smuggled advanced AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with Jensen Huang.

In their Sunday statement, the board said that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets” were compromised by Jensen Huang’s relationship with accused Chinese spy.

“The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” the company added in the statement.

The Nvidia CEO recently acknowledged that he has been unfaithful to his wife, adding “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” according to a Sunday report from Bloomberg .

He has been called to appear by a group of GOP lawmakers in a joint, closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 to address concerns regarding Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with … Alice Huang.”
